summary: Instructions for the continually tended lamp and twelve weekly bread cakes give way to a rare narrative: a man curses the divine Name during a fight and is held while Moses seeks a ruling. The resulting speech gives a death penalty for blasphemy, rules for homicide and injury, equal law for foreigner and native-born, and ends with the man's execution.
whyItMatters: The chapter moves from maintaining holy space to guarding the divine name and judging harm within the camp. Its equal-law formula includes both legal protection and exposure to the severe penalties described.

context.author: Leviticus presents the instructions and ruling as Yahweh's speech to Moses; the finished book does not name its narrator, and its composition history remains debated.
context.audience: The children of Israel provide oil, hear the ruling, and carry it out; Aaron tends the lamp and bread, and the same legal standard names foreigner and native-born.
context.date: The narrative is set in Israel's Sinai camp; the date of the book's received literary form is debated.
context.setting: The Tent of Meeting and the surrounding camp, followed by an execution outside the camp.
context.literaryForm: Sanctuary instruction followed by legal narrative, divine ruling, talionic injury law, and reported execution.

outline.heading: Oil for the continual lamp
outline.note: Israel supplies pure oil, and Aaron tends the lamps from evening to morning.

outline.heading: Twelve cakes before Yahweh
outline.note: Bread and frankincense are arranged each Sabbath before becoming a most holy priestly portion.

outline.heading: A fight, a curse, and custody
outline.note: A man with an Israelite mother and Egyptian father blasphemes the Name and is detained until a ruling is given.

outline.heading: The blasphemy ruling
outline.note: Witnesses lay hands on the man, and the same capital rule is stated for foreigner and native-born.

outline.heading: Homicide, injury, and equal law
outline.note: Human killing, animal loss, and bodily injury receive distinct but proportionate formulas under one legal standard.

outline.heading: The sentence carried out
outline.note: Israel takes the man outside the camp and stones him as Moses had commanded.

keyVerses.text: Every Sabbath day he shall set it in order before Yahweh continually. It is an everlasting covenant on the behalf of the children of Israel.
keyVerses.why: The bread is arranged every Sabbath as a continuing covenant observance.

keyVerses.text: He who blasphemes Yahweh’s name, he shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall certainly stone him. The foreigner as well as the native-born shall be put to death when he blasphemes the Name.
keyVerses.why: The ruling explicitly prescribes stoning for blasphemy, including foreigner and native-born.

keyVerses.text: You shall have one kind of law for the foreigner as well as the native-born; for I am Yahweh your God.’”
keyVerses.why: One legal standard governs the two groups within this legal unit.

themes: one law for foreigner and native-born

questions.question: What do the lamp and bread instructions require?
questions.answer: Israel supplies pure beaten olive oil, Aaron tends the lamps from evening to morning, and twelve cakes are arranged with frankincense every Sabbath. The bread then belongs to Aaron and his sons to eat in a holy place as a most holy portion.

questions.question: What does “continually” mean for the lamp and bread?
questions.answer: For the lamp, Aaron keeps it ordered from evening to morning as a continuing generational statute. For the bread, he renews its ordered display every Sabbath, so the word describes faithfully recurring service rather than one object remaining untouched forever.

questions.question: Why does the narrative identify the man's parents?
questions.answer: It locates him in the camp as the son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian father, but the text does not blame his ancestry for the offense or explain why his lineage is narrated. The ruling later applies one legal standard to foreigner and native-born rather than assigning a different standard by resident status.

questions.question: What does it mean that he blasphemed “the Name”?
questions.answer: Verse 11 says he blasphemed the Name and cursed, and verse 16 identifies the name as Yahweh’s. The offense is directed at the divine name; the narrative does not preserve the man’s exact words.

questions.question: Why is the man held in custody before sentencing?
questions.answer: Verse 12 says the community waits until Yahweh's will is declared rather than improvising a penalty during the conflict. The pause is narratively important even though the resulting ruling and execution remain severe and troubling.

questions.question: What is commanded and then carried out in the blasphemy case?
questions.answer: Those who heard the curse are commanded to lay their hands on the man’s head, and the whole congregation is to stone him outside the camp. The final verse reports that he is taken out and stoned as commanded. This is an actual execution in the narrative, following the newly given ruling.

questions.question: What does the “eye for eye” formula say?
questions.answer: The law says the injury is to be done to the offender as it was done to the neighbor: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, and tooth for tooth. Beside it, killing an animal requires replacement, while killing a human requires death. The formula describes matching harm but gives no further procedure or compensation schedule here.

questions.question: What does one law for foreigner and native-born accomplish?
questions.answer: It rejects different injury or blasphemy standards based on resident status within this legal unit. The equality includes exposure to the chapter's severe penalties, not only protection, so the statement is both an equal-treatment rule and part of a violent ancient code.

glossary.def: The narrative’s designation for Yahweh’s divine name, which the man is said to curse.
The sanctuary designation associated here with the veil outside which Aaron tends the lamp.
The role assigned to frankincense placed with the twelve bread cakes before Yahweh.
The formula attached to replacement for an animal killed, within the chapter's larger proportional-response unit.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: The sacred calendar closes with the Feast of Booths and its remembrance of the exodus. The next instructions focus on the regular service of lamps and bread at the Tent.

here.text: Sanctuary routines give way to a camp dispute, custody, a divine ruling, and execution. The ruling also distinguishes homicide, animal loss, and bodily injury under one law for foreigner and native-born.

after.text: The following speech extends Sabbath rest to the land and introduces Jubilee, redemption of property and Israelite debt servants, and the sharply different rule permitting permanent foreign slavery.
